speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) over the past three years, how many cases are there of domestic helpers who have defaulted on loans from licensed moneylenders; (b) whether the Ministry intends to implement any restrictions on domestic helpers taking such loans; (c) what are the consequences for such repeat defaulters; and (d) what are the consequences for their employers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) over the past three years, how many domestic helpers have taken loans from unlicensed moneylenders; (b) what are the consequences for such domestic helpers; and (c) what recourse do the employers of these domestic helpers have should they be harassed by the unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: asked the Minister for Law (a) what is the number of foreign domestic workers who have procured loans from licensed moneylenders in 2017 and 2018; (b) what are the liabilities for employers of foreign domestic workers who default on repayment of such loans; and (c) whether the Ministry has any plans to place any restrictions on foreign domestic workers procuring such loans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Senior Minister of State for Law Mr Edwin Tong will address the remaining parts of the questions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Where licensed moneylending is concerned, FDWs who do not repay their loans may be subject to civil action by licensed moneylenders, as with any other borrowers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Employers of FDWs are not liable to repay any of their FDWs' loans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is an offence for licensed moneylenders to harass the FDWs or their employers for repayment or employ an agent to do so.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: FDW employers who are harassed should report to the Police.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We do not condone any borrowing from unlicensed moneylenders by foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We will intensify efforts to help them learn about money management and the risks of borrowing from moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Any person who is harassed by unlicensed moneylenders should report such activities to the Police.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: From 2008 to September 2018, the Police registered about 460 reports of harassment by unlicensed moneylenders arising from FDWs borrowing or acting as guarantors.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Police and Attorney-General’s Chambers have prosecuted errant debt collectors who have violated the law and will continue to take strong enforcement action against such conduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Darryl David and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked for statistics on FDWs who have taken loans from licensed and unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr David and Mr Sitoh also asked if the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) intends to place any restrictions on FDWs taking such loans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moneylending regulations do not formally define a "loan default".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, estimates based on Moneylenders Credit Bureau (MLCB) data from 2016 to the first half of 2018 show that the majority of FDWs have repaid their loans from licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Police have also observed more foreigners residing in Singapore, including FDWs, borrowing from unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are currently several measures to protect all individuals who borrow from licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, the Moneylenders Rules permit a licensed moneylender to charge only the following for each loan: (a) an upfront administrative fee of up to 10%; (b) interest of up to 4% per month; (c) late interest of up to 4% per month; and (d) late fees of up to $60 per month.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Registrar of Moneylenders had issued Directions to regulate moneylenders' activities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, moneylenders are prohibited from advertising their loans to members of the public via mobile text messages or emails.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Moneylenders are also prohibited from conducting abusive practices, such as repeatedly "rolling over" existing loans to charge the administrative fee multiple times even though no new credit is issued; or offering split loans so that late fees can be charged multiple times, per loan, each month.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the Ministry will impose aggregate loan caps to limit the total amount that any foreigner residing in Singapore can borrow from licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The caps were first announced for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents under the Moneylenders (Amendment) Bill in January this year, and the caps are: (a) individuals earning up to $20,000 a year may borrow up to $3,000; and (b) individuals earning $20,000 or more a year may borrow up to six times of their monthly income.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both caps will be extended to all foreigners residing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the Ministry will also introduce a self-exclusion framework for all individuals who borrow from licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both Singapore residents and foreigners may apply for self-exclusion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Licensed moneylenders will be prohibited from lending to self-excluded individuals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This framework will help individuals to control their borrowing habits and to participate in debt assistance schemes administered by voluntary welfare organisations which typically also require self-exclusion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MinLaw, together with MOM and the Singapore Police Force, will continue to monitor the situation following the implementation of these measures and will assess if more stringent measures are necessary.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is heartening to hear that there are measures that are being taken with regard to self-exclusion and the caps.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would it be useful for the Government to consider, perhaps in light of the fact that the employers are usually the ones who have to suffer the consequences should FDWs default on their licensed moneylending loans, to have a practice where the employer's consent needs to be sought before FDWs approach licensed moneylenders for loans?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, in a way, if you look at the self-exclusion for the casinos, for example, I understand that family members can also choose to exclude certain family members.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, my question is, can the authorities consider with the case of licensed moneylenders, for the employer's consent to be sought before the FDW makes that loan with the licensed moneylender?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second supplementary question is relating to the issue of unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As far as I understand it right now, it is not an offence to take a loan from an unlicensed moneylender.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not legal for a moneylender to carry out a business without a licence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: With that clarification, Mr Deputy Speaker, what usually happens then is that perhaps if the FDW makes that loan and she then has her employment terminated by the employer – understandably, when the employer finds out – she returns.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As she has committed no crime, the FDW is technically able to return to the country again and perhaps, this entire cycle is repeated by which the FDW then perpetuates further inconvenience and stress on her new employer.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Would the authorities consider perhaps in such cases some measure – I understand the concept of innocent until proven guilty – whereby such FDWs are either placed on a watchlist or even barred from returning until this matter can be clarified, to avoid further inconveniences down the road?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we are not studying it, can I ask whether MOM is willing to conduct this study so that we understand what the root of the problem is, and then we can really address it?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to thank Member Mr Louis Ng for his question.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Yes, we have been looking into all the possible reasons.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They need to borrow this amount of money for a month before they receive their next pay cheque from the employers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are thinking through and we will certainly consider mounting a study to understand this a little more.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And not to mention FDWs, but even my residents would receive short message service (SMS) from unlicensed moneylenders and they just go ahead to borrow money from them.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The measure of sending the FDWs back seems very drastic because the FDW may not know.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can we exercise some flexibility so that, with the consent of the employer, they can actually continue to stay in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For employers who wish to continue hiring their FDWs who are debarred for various reasons – maybe because they are pending the arrival of a new FDW – they can certainly put in a request to MOM, and we will look at it on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
